sections.title: Controller and reliever
sections.text: For moderate-to-severe persistent asthma in people aged at least four years, NAEPP recommends ICS-formoterol as both maintenance and relief therapy.

sections.title: SMART boundaries
sections.text: The SMART evidence concerns formoterol. ICS-salmeterol maintenance should not be paired with ICS-formoterol as its reliever.

sections.title: Add-on treatment
sections.text: When ICS alone is insufficient, adding a LABA is preferred to adding a LAMA; a LAMA is an alternative when LABA cannot be used.

sections.title: FeNO as an adjunct
sections.text: For people aged five years or older whose asthma diagnosis remains uncertain after history, examination and spirometry with bronchodilator testing, NAEPP conditionally supports adding FeNO to the evaluation. FeNO is an adjunct, not a stand-alone assessment of asthma control, future exacerbations or exacerbation severity.
sections.sourceLocator: Printed pages 8–9; FeNO diagnostic recommendations and management key points.

sections.title: Targeted indoor allergen reduction
sections.text: When asthma is associated with sensitivity to indoor allergens such as dust mites, NHLBI describes using multiple allergen-reduction strategies. A mattress or pillow cover alone often does not improve asthma outcomes. Routine indoor allergen interventions are not recommended for people without relevant indoor allergy.
sections.sourceLocator: Indoor Allergen Reduction bullets: multiple strategies and absence of indoor allergy.

sections.title: Diagnostic confirmation
sections.text: VA/DoD suggests post-bronchodilator spirometry to confirm a clinical COPD diagnosis.

sections.title: Risk reduction
sections.text: Smoking cessation with complete abstinence is recommended. Respiratory vaccination is also suggested to reduce exacerbation risk.

sections.title: Maintenance selection
sections.text: For significant symptom burden, LABA/LAMA combination is recommended over monotherapy. Prior-year exacerbations requiring steroids or antibiotics support ICS/LABA/LAMA triple therapy.

sections.title: Pulmonary rehabilitation
sections.text: CDC describes pulmonary rehabilitation as a personalized program that teaches COPD symptom-management strategies, including breathing techniques, energy conservation, and appropriate food and physical activity choices. COPD can be treated to improve symptoms and quality of life, but these measures do not constitute a cure.
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment and management; Lifestyle changes: pulmonary rehabilitation; opening statement that COPD has no cure.

sections.title: Smoking cessation priority
sections.text: For a person with COPD who smokes, CDC identifies stopping smoking as the most important part of treatment. Respiratory vaccinations and appropriate medication are additional management measures. Supplemental oxygen is discussed for low blood oxygen, not as a universal substitute for smoking cessation.
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment and management: Lifestyle changes, quit smoking; Treatment options, vaccines and oxygen.

sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: Adult CAP assessment combines a new imaging infiltrate with respiratory symptoms and another compatible clinical finding.

sections.title: Severe disease
sections.text: Vasopressor-dependent septic shock or respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation is a major severe-CAP criterion.

sections.title: Nonsevere inpatient treatment
sections.text: Without MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors, a beta-lactam plus macrolide is a preferred inpatient regimen; a respiratory fluoroquinolone is another pathway option.

sections.title: Initial diagnostic imaging
sections.text: NHLBI explains that pneumonia diagnosis combines history, examination and tests. A chest X-ray is commonly used to look for lung inflammation. Pulse oximetry assesses blood oxygen rather than providing lung imaging. CT provides more detail and can reveal complications; it is not described as necessary for every patient.
sections.sourceLocator: Diagnostic tests and procedures: chest X-ray, pulse oximetry and chest CT.

sections.title: Pleural fluid evaluation
sections.text: When pleural fluid sampling is indicated, thoracentesis obtains fluid from the pleural space between the lung and chest wall for culture. Bronchoscopy examines the airways and may collect lung tissue or lung fluid when pneumonia treatment is not working well. CT can demonstrate pleural disorders but does not itself obtain a culture specimen.
sections.sourceLocator: Diagnostic tests and procedures: bronchoscopy, chest CT and pleural fluid culture/thoracentesis.

sections.title: Assessment
sections.text: Assess vitals and lungs for pneumonia.

sections.title: Sputum interpretation
sections.text: Sputum color does not prove bacterial infection.

sections.title: Antibiotic stewardship
sections.text: No routine antibiotics, irrespective of cough duration.

sections.title: Chest imaging in uncomplicated cough
sections.text: CDC describes pneumonia as uncommon in otherwise healthy adults without abnormal vital signs or focal lung findings. Relevant abnormalities include heart rate at least 100, respiratory rate at least 24, oral temperature at least 38°C, or focal consolidation, egophony or fremitus. Chest radiography is not indicated in most uncomplicated bronchitis cases.

sections.title: Symptom relief versus cure
sections.text: CDC describes rest and fluids as supportive measures for uncomplicated acute bronchitis. Over-the-counter medicines may temporarily relieve symptoms, but they do not cure the illness. Product labels and directions still apply, and medication selection should account for other prescription and nonprescription medicines.

sections.text: First-line antibiotics: amoxicillin/amoxicillin-clavulanate; avoid azithromycin because of resistance.

sections.title: First-line antibiotic selection
sections.text: When an adult bacterial rhinosinusitis case is selected for antibiotic treatment, CDC lists amoxicillin or amoxicillin/clavulanate as first-line agents. Macrolides such as azithromycin are not recommended because of pneumococcal resistance. Doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone are listed alternatives for penicillin-allergic patients; they are not presented as the default first-line choice for every adult.

sections.title: Clinical patterns and imaging
sections.text: CDC supports bacterial rhinosinusitis recognition using persistent symptoms beyond ten days without improvement, severe symptoms, or deterioration after initial improvement. sections.title: Testing indications
sections.text: Clear viral features obviate GAS testing. Without such features, examination alone cannot reliably distinguish GAS from viral pharyngitis.

sections.title: Negative rapid test
sections.text: A symptomatic child aged at least three years needs a throat culture after a negative RADT; adults do not routinely need that backup.

sections.title: Confirmed infection
sections.text: A positive RADT or culture warrants antibiotics. Penicillin or amoxicillin is preferred when appropriate.

sections.title: Clear viral features
sections.text: Cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, oral ulcers or conjunctivitis strongly suggest viral pharyngitis. When clear viral symptoms are present, CDC says history and examination can support a viral diagnosis without GAS testing. Antibiotics should not treat viral pharyngitis.

sections.title: Immediate penicillin hypersensitivity
sections.text: CDC specifically advises avoiding cephalexin and cefadroxil in patients with immediate-type penicillin hypersensitivity. sections.title: Testing and ulcer history
sections.text: Current or previous peptic ulcer disease is an indication to assess H. pylori when prior eradication is not established.

sections.title: Treatment selection
sections.text: Optimized bismuth quadruple treatment is recommended empirically. Avoid clarithromycin- or levofloxacin-containing regimens without demonstrated susceptibility.

sections.title: Confirming eradication
sections.text: Confirm cure at least four weeks after therapy using breath, stool-antigen or biopsy testing. Hold PPIs two weeks and antibiotics/bismuth four weeks to avoid false negatives.

sections.title: Managing an NSAID contributor
sections.text: For an NSAID-associated ulcer, NIDDK describes clinician-directed changes to the NSAID or pain medicine. If an NSAID must continue, a PPI may be recommended. Ulcer healing includes addressing the cause, not only symptoms.

sections.text: Maintained HIV RNA below 200 copies/mL with ART prevents sexual transmission.

sections.title: Routine HIV screening and consent
sections.text: CDC recommends that all patients aged 13–64 receive HIV testing at least once as part of routine health care, with at least annual screening for ongoing risk factors. An opt-out approach means informing the patient that testing will be included and allowing the patient to decline; it does not mean testing secretly or without the opportunity to refuse.
sections.sourceLocator: Key points; Screening recommendations and opt-out approach.

sections.title: A negative initial test can require HIV RNA
sections.text: When acute HIV is suspected after a recent possible exposure and initial CDC-algorithm tests are negative or indeterminate, CDC recommends additional HIV RNA testing. If RNA is also negative, repeat testing in a few weeks is recommended to assess very early infection. A negative antibody or antigen/antibody report must not be assumed to include an RNA test.

Obtain an antibody-only home test as the sole assessment
Obtain a CD4 count alone

questions.stem: A fictional 22-year-old attending routine primary care has never been tested for HIV and reports no ongoing risk factor. Which CDC screening approach is appropriate?

sections.title: Nonpregnant adult treatment
sections.text: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for seven days is recommended for uncomplicated adolescent and adult infection outside pregnancy.

sections.title: Partner management
sections.text: Recent sex partners need evaluation and treatment. Abstain until the regimen is complete, symptoms resolve and partners are treated.

sections.title: Follow-up
sections.text: Retest approximately three months after treatment for reinfection. Routine four-week test of cure is not indicated in nonpregnant adherent patients without ongoing symptoms or reinfection concern.

sections.title: Pregnancy requires a test of cure
sections.text: For chlamydial infection in pregnancy, CDC recommends a test of cure, preferably by NAAT, approximately 4 weeks after completion of treatment. Retesting at 3 months also addresses reinfection. The pregnancy requirement must not be replaced by the ordinary nonpregnant rule against routine test of cure.
sections.sourceLocator: Special Considerations — Pregnancy, test-of-cure and retesting paragraph.

sections.title: Screening without symptoms and specimen choice
sections.text: CDC recommends annual chlamydia screening for sexually active women younger than 25 years and older women with increased risk. NAAT is recommended for detecting urogenital infection. A patient-collected vaginal swab in a clinical setting is an acceptable specimen approach; its sensitivity and specificity are equivalent to clinician-collected vaginal swabs.
sections.sourceLocator: Chlamydial Infection Among Adolescents and Adults, annual-screening paragraph; Diagnostic Considerations, vaginal-swab NAAT paragraphs.

Weekly testing forever

Use only the 3-month reinfection retest with no earlier test of cure
Obtain the pregnancy test of cure by NAAT 2 weeks after completing therapy
Obtain a test of cure, preferably by NAAT, approximately 4 weeks after completing therapy

distractorExplanations.E: That applies the ordinary nonpregnant follow-up condition instead of the separate pregnancy recommendation.

questions.stem: A fictional sexually active 21-year-old woman has no genitourinary symptoms and is due for chlamydia screening. She prefers to collect her own vaginal swab in the clinic. Which plan follows CDC guidance?

Use urinalysis alone rather than a chlamydia NAAT

sections.title: Uncomplicated infection
sections.text: Use ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once when weight is below 150 kg; use 1 g at 150 kg or above. Address chlamydia if it has not been excluded.

sections.title: Pharyngeal follow-up
sections.text: Pharyngeal gonorrhea needs a test of cure seven to fourteen days after initial treatment; uncomplicated treated anogenital infection does not routinely require this.

sections.title: Reinfection prevention
sections.text: Retest about three months after treatment and ensure recent partners receive evaluation and treatment.

sections.title: Persistent symptoms need culture and susceptibility assessment
sections.text: CDC says to consider treatment failure when symptoms persist 3–5 days after recommended gonorrhea treatment and no posttreatment sexual contact is reported. Most suspected failures are reinfections, but when reinfection is unlikely and failure is suspected, obtain relevant specimens for culture, preferably with simultaneous NAAT, and susceptibility testing if gonorrhea is isolated before retreatment. Specialist/public-health consultation is part of this pathway.
sections.sourceLocator: Suspected Cephalosporin Treatment Failure, recognition, culture/susceptibility and consultation paragraphs.

sections.title: Disseminated disease can have little genital inflammation
sections.text: Disseminated gonococcal infection can cause acral petechial or pustular lesions, asymmetric polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis or oligoarticular septic arthritis, while genital infection can be minimally symptomatic. When DGI is suspected, CDC recommends NAAT and culture from exposed urogenital/extragenital sites and from disseminated sites of infection; gonococcal isolates should receive susceptibility testing.

questions.stem: A fictional adult has persistent gonorrhea symptoms 5 days after recommended treatment, reports no sexual contact afterward, and reinfection is judged unlikely. Before choosing retreatment, which investigation best follows the CDC suspected-failure pathway?

choices.text: Repeat NAAT alone without obtaining culture or susceptibility information
Obtain relevant culture specimens, preferably with simultaneous NAAT, and susceptibility testing if gonorrhea is isolated
Use a urethral Gram stain alone to infer antibiotic susceptibility
Obtain culture but omit susceptibility testing if gonorrhea is isolated
Defer investigation to the routine 3-month NAAT reinfection retest

questions.explanation: CDC recommends culture and susceptibility assessment before retreatment when failure is suspected and reinfection is unlikely. Persistent symptoms do not themselves prove resistant infection.

distractorExplanations.A: The suspected-failure pathway specifically calls for culture and susceptibility assessment when reinfection is unlikely.
distractorExplanations.C: The source calls for testing gonococcal isolates for susceptibility rather than inferring it from microscopy alone.
distractorExplanations.D: Susceptibility testing of the isolate is part of the stated CDC suspected-failure investigation.
distractorExplanations.E: The ongoing symptoms and unlikely reinfection fit the source failure-assessment pathway, not delayed routine screening.

questions.learningObjective: Investigate suspected gonorrhea treatment failure without prematurely labeling resistance.

questions.stem: In a fictional study case, an adult has pustular acral lesions, tenosynovitis and asymmetric joint pain after a possible STI exposure, but little genital discomfort. DGI is suspected. Which testing approach fits CDC guidance?

choices.text: Obtain only a genital NAAT because genital infection is the presumed entry site
Culture blood or an involved joint without assessing exposed mucosal sites
Obtain NAAT from exposed mucosal sites but no cultures or disseminated-site specimens
Culture only one skin lesion and omit the remaining exposed and disseminated sites
Test exposed mucosal sites and disseminated infection sites using the recommended NAAT/culture approach

questions.explanation: DGI may occur with minimal genital inflammation. CDC recommends testing exposed urogenital/extragenital sites and disseminated sites, with susceptibility testing for gonococcal isolates.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC calls for exposed urogenital/extragenital sites and disseminated infection sites, even when genital symptoms are minimal.
distractorExplanations.B: The source also includes exposed mucosal sites in the DGI investigation.
distractorExplanations.C: The source recommends both site categories and culture information; this samples only part of the suspected DGI presentation.
distractorExplanations.D: Testing only that lesion omits the broader source-directed site assessment.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize a disseminated gonococcal pattern and broaden site-specific diagnostic sampling.
